summary: Provides the XDR description for NFS version 4 minor version 1, the formal data encoding used for its messages.

plainLanguage.summary:
NFS lets a computer use files stored on a server as if they were local. This document does not describe how NFS behaves; it describes exactly how the bits of every NFS message are laid out.

The description is written in XDR, a notation in which each field has a type and a length, so that a computer of any kind can read the same bytes the same way. The whole description is written so that a short script can pull it out of the document and turn it into a file that a compiler can use directly.

subtitle: The machine-readable description of the data formats used by NFS version 4.1, written in XDR.

tldr.problem: NFS version 4.1 has a large and precise set of message formats: dozens of operations, each with its own arguments and results. Writing them out in prose in the protocol document would be unreadable and easy to get wrong, and implementers would still have to translate the prose into machine-readable form.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC writes the formats directly in XDR, the notation of RFC 4506, and marks every line of the description with a sentinel so that a small shell script can extract the whole thing from the document into a file called nfs4_prot.x.
tldr.outcome: The description also covers the operations and features of NFSv4.0 that do not apply to NFSv4.1, so that an implementation supporting both versions can use one file. The protocol specification itself, RFC 5661, points here for the security and IANA considerations.

facts.label: First operation number added in NFSv4.1

today: RFC 5662 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It provides the XDR description that the NFS version 4 minor version 1 protocol specification in RFC 5661 depends on, and it also covers the NFSv4.0 operations that did not change in version 4.1.

sections.title: What This Document Provides
sections.content:
This document provides the External Data Representation Standard (XDR) description for Network File System version 4 (NFSv4) minor version 1. XDR itself is the notation and encoding described in RFC 4506.

In order to facilitate implementations that support both NFSv4.0 and NFSv4.1, the description includes operations and other features of NFSv4.0 that do not apply to NFSv4.1.

The XDR description and the scripts for extracting it are Code Components, as described in the Legal Provisions Relating to IETF Documents. The protocol specification that this description belongs to is RFC 5661, and the description was derived from the earlier descriptions in RFC 3530 and RFC 5661.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a companion document to the NFSv4.1 protocol specification. It contains no behaviour of its own; it is the exact layout of the data, so that two implementations written by different people agree on what the bytes mean.

sections.title: How the Description Is Written and Extracted
sections.content:
The XDR description is provided in the document in a way that makes it simple for the reader to extract into ready-to-compile form. The shell script in the document greps for lines beginning with the sentinel sequence of three slashes and strips it, along with the leading white space, from each line:

#!/bin/sh
grep '^ *///' | sed 's?^ */// ??' | sed 's?^ *///$??'

With that script stored in a file called extract.sh and the document in a file called spec.txt, the reader runs:

sh extract.sh < spec.txt > nfs4_prot.x

The effect of the script is to remove the leading white space from each line, plus the sentinel sequence. The result is the machine-readable XDR description of NFSv4.1, in the form of an XDR language definition file for the protocol interface, which is what a compiler such as rpcgen turns into client and server stubs.
sections.plainLanguage: Every line of the description starts with three slashes. A script that keeps only those lines and removes the slashes turns the document into a clean definition file. The result can be handed straight to the usual XDR tools.

sections.title: Operations, Compounds and the Callback Program
sections.content:
The description defines an enumeration nfs_opnum4 of the operation numbers, and two unions that pair each operation with its arguments and its results: nfs_argop4 switches on the operation number and carries the matching argument structure, and nfs_resop4 does the same for results.

The operations inherited from NFSv4.0 run from OP_ACCESS at 3 to OP_RELEASE_LOCKOWNER at 39. Several of them are marked in the description as mandatory not-to-implement: OP_OPEN_CONFIRM at 20, OP_RENEW at 30, OP_SETCLIENTID at 35, OP_SETCLIENTID_CONFIRM at 36 and OP_RELEASE_LOCKOWNER at 39.

NFSv4.1 adds its own operations, numbered from 40 to 58, and an OP_ILLEGAL value of 10044. The new operations are OP_BACKCHANNEL_CTL at 40, OP_BIND_CONN_TO_SESSION at 41, OP_EXCHANGE_ID at 42, OP_CREATE_SESSION at 43, OP_DESTROY_SESSION at 44, OP_FREE_STATEID at 45, OP_GET_DIR_DELEGATION at 46, OP_GETDEVICEINFO at 47, OP_GETDEVICELIST at 48, OP_LAYOUTCOMMIT at 49, OP_LAYOUTGET at 50, OP_LAYOUTRETURN at 51, OP_SECINFO_NO_NAME at 52, OP_SEQUENCE at 53, OP_SET_SSV at 54, OP_TEST_STATEID at 55, OP_WANT_DELEGATION at 56, OP_DESTROY_CLIENTID at 57 and OP_RECLAIM_COMPLETE at 58.

Everything travels inside a compound call. COMPOUND4args carries a tag, a minor version number and an array of argument operations; COMPOUND4res carries a status, a tag and an array of result operations. The RPC program NFS4_PROGRAM has a single version NFS_V4 with two procedures: NFSPROC4_NULL at 0 and NFSPROC4_COMPOUND at 1.

A second program, NFS4_CALLBACK, carries the messages the server sends back to a client, such as a delegation recall. It has one version, NFS_CB, with the procedures CB_NULL at 0 and CB_COMPOUND at 1, and its own argument and result unions nfs_cb_argop4 and nfs_cb_resop4. The callback operations are OP_CB_GETATTR, OP_CB_RECALL, OP_CB_LAYOUTRECALL, which is new to NFSv4.1, OP_CB_NOTIFY, OP_CB_PUSH_DELEG, OP_CB_RECALL_ANY, OP_CB_RECALLABLE_OBJ_AVAIL, OP_CB_RECALL_SLOT, OP_CB_SEQUENCE, OP_CB_WANTS_CANCELLED, OP_CB_NOTIFY_LOCK, OP_CB_NOTIFY_DEVICEID and OP_CB_ILLEGAL at 10044. The program number is in the transient range, since the client assigns the exact transient program number and provides that to the server through the SETCLIENTID operation.
sections.plainLanguage:
The description names every operation the protocol can carry and gives each one a number. NFSv4.0 used numbers 3 to 39; NFSv4.1 added the numbers 40 to 58.

A client sends a list of operations in one compound call, and the server answers with a matching list of results. A second, separate program carries the messages that flow the other way, from the server to the client.

sections.title: Sizes, Identifiers and Attribute Bits
sections.content:
The description begins with a set of constants that fix the sizes involved. A file handle is at most 128 bytes, the verifier is 8 bytes, an opaque field is at most 1024 bytes, and a session identifier is 16 bytes. There are also the largest and smallest values for the integer types: NFS4_INT64_MAX, NFS4_UINT64_MAX, NFS4_INT32_MAX, NFS4_UINT32_MAX, plus NFS4_MAXFILELEN and NFS4_MAXFILEOFF.

The basic typedefs follow. attrlist4 and bitmap4 are opaque and variable-length, changeid4 and clientid4 are 64-bit, count4 and mode4 are 32-bit, length4 and nfs_cookie4 are 64-bit, offset4 and sequenceid4 are 32-bit, and utf8string has three variants for case-sensitive, case-insensitive and mixed text.

Two enumerations give the vocabulary of the protocol. The file types nfs_ftype4 run from NF4REG at 1, a regular file, through NF4DIR for a directory, NF4BLK and NF4CHR for devices, NF4LNK for a symbolic link, NF4SOCK for a socket and NF4FIFO for a named pipe, to NF4ATTRDIR at 8 and NF4NAMEDATTR at 9. The error codes nfsstat4 start at NFS4_OK for 0 and run through the ordinary Unix-style errors such as NFS4ERR_NOENT for 2 and NFS4ERR_ACCESS for 13, then through NFSv4-specific ones such as NFS4ERR_BADHANDLE at 10001 and NFS4ERR_OP_ILLEGAL at 10044. The description notes that value 19 must not be allocated, because it was used in NFSv3 and must not change meaning in NFSv4.

The stateid4 structure is a 32-bit sequence number followed by 12 other bytes, and it is the value the server hands back to identify an open, a delegation or a lock. A verifier is 8 bytes of opaque data.

File attributes are not separate structures but numbered bits in a bitmap, so that a client can ask for exactly the attributes it needs. The required attributes are numbered from 0: FATTR4_SUPPORTED_ATTRS at 0, FATTR4_TYPE at 1, FATTR4_FH_EXPIRE_TYPE at 2, FATTR4_CHANGE at 3, FATTR4_SIZE at 4, FATTR4_LINK_SUPPORT at 5, FATTR4_SYMLINK_SUPPORT at 6, FATTR4_NAMED_ATTR at 7, FATTR4_FSID at 8, FATTR4_UNIQUE_HANDLES at 9, FATTR4_LEASE_TIME at 10 and FATTR4_RDATTR_ERROR at 11, with FATTR4_FILEHANDLE at 19 and the new-to-NFSv4.1 FATTR4_SUPPATTR_EXCLCREAT at 75. The recommended attributes include FATTR4_ACL at 12, FATTR4_ACLSUPPORT at 13, FATTR4_ARCHIVE at 14, FATTR4_CANSETTIME at 15, FATTR4_CASE_INSENSITIVE at 16 and FATTR4_CASE_PRESERVING at 17.
sections.plainLanguage:
The description fixes the sizes of the opaque values: a file handle can be up to 128 bytes, a session identifier is 16 bytes, and a verifier is 8.

Attributes are the interesting part. Instead of a fixed record of every possible property of a file, each property has a number, and the client sends a bitmap of the numbers it wants. That is why a client that only needs the size and the modification time does not have to receive the owner, the permissions and the quota information as well.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations are those of the protocol specification itself, given in the Security Considerations section of RFC 5661. This document defines data formats rather than behaviour, so it adds none of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The document describes data formats only, so it has no security rules of its own. Those are set out in the NFSv4.1 protocol specification.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The IANA considerations are those of the protocol specification itself, given in the IANA Considerations section of RFC 5661.
sections.plainLanguage: The same applies to the registrations this description relies on: they are made in the protocol specification, not here.
